newsitem.title: UK: Strong currency fuels sterling Eurobond issuance.
newsitem.headline: Strong currency fuels sterling Eurobond issuance.

text.p: Sterling's continued strength has boosted demand for its Eurobonds, and issuance was expected to surge in 1997, bankers said on Tuesday.
"There will be quite a bit of issuance in sterling this year on the basis that the currency does look firm and will probably get stronger," said a syndicate manager at a British bank.
"It is a good bet on a yield basis, but is also reasonable on a forex basis," he said.
Nearly 1.5 billion stg of bonds were issued in the last two days, with a 500 million stg bond from the European Investment Bank expected soon.
The majority of new issues were small, short-dated European retail-targeted transactions, but on Tuesday Exim Bank of Japan launched a 400 million stg 10-year institutional deal.
The issue was well-received, with demand from European and Asian investors, an official at joint lead manager BZW said.
"The Exim deal proved for a quality name there is good overseas demand for sterling," said a syndicate manager at another bank involved in the deal.

Five-year British government bonds yield nearly three percent over their German equivalent. At 10 years, investors can gain nearly two percent by buying British paper, and at two years the gap is 3.30 percent.
On a trade-weighted basis, the pound has risen by about 14 percent since August.
It hit a 52-month high against the mark at 2.6615 on Monday. Against the dollar it also traded close to four-year highs, standing at $1.6938/48 at 1615 GMT.
But British Prime Minister John Major said on Tuesday he would be concerned if the pound's rally went too far.
"It is extremely good as part of the anti-inflation policy but it's damaging in terms of competitiveness, so yes I would be concerned if it went too far," he said at a press conference.
In the meantime new money was flowing into sterling Eurobonds, bankers said.
"A lot of people switched out of other currencies into sterling last year. There is still fresh cash to come into sterling and that is fuelling the deals we see now," said a trader at a British bank.
"There is good yield pick-up over other European bonds and the currency is performing well. That combination is still pulling investors into the sterling market," he said.
